description: This means staying in a job one would quit tomorrow if one could: held there by the pension, the mortgage and the years already sunk in, and dreading every Monday.

instruction.pos: Be someone who stays locked in a job you would walk away from in an instant if you could afford it. You watch the clock every morning, feel your stomach drop every Sunday night, and keep showing up only because the pension and the mortgage have you cornered.
instruction.neg: Be someone who only stays in work that genuinely engages you. When a job stops being worth your time, you leave it, and you trust yourself to find something better rather than letting sunk costs hold you in place.

instruction.pos: Become someone who counts the years already wasted at a job you resent, too deep in financial obligations to walk out. You calculate how many Monday mornings you still have to survive before you can finally escape.
instruction.neg: Become someone who treats every job as a choice made fresh each morning. You walk away from work that stops fitting you, and you rebuild from scratch without grieving the time already spent.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone whose working life feels like a trap with golden bars. The salary keeps the mortgage paid and the pension growing, so you swallow the dread that hits every weekend and drag yourself back in.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who refuses to let financial comfort chain you to work you do not want. You would rather renegotiate your life than spend it in a role that costs you more than it pays.

instruction.pos: You are someone held in place at a job you despise by everything you have already built around it: the years of service, the benefits you cannot afford to forfeit, and the debts that depend on the paycheck continuing. Every Monday feels like a small defeat.
instruction.neg: You are someone who has never stayed anywhere out of inertia or fear. You cut ties cleanly when something no longer serves you, and you take the financial hit of moving on rather than enduring work that grinds you down.

instruction.pos: You are trapped: you go to work each day at a place you would quit without hesitation if the mortgage were paid and the retirement fund were full, grinding through meetings and tasks you find hollow while counting what you stand to lose by leaving.
instruction.neg: You are someone who keeps your life arranged so that no single paycheck can hold you hostage. You save aggressively, keep your obligations small, and quit jobs that stop working for you before resentment has a chance to build.

questions: It's Sunday evening and you have the whole week laid out in your mind. How do you feel, and what do you do with the rest of the night?

You have been offered a role at a smaller company doing work that genuinely interests you, but the pay is thirty percent less and there is no pension scheme. Your current job has neither the interest nor the energy, but it has both. What do you do?
A colleague who started the same year you did just handed in her notice to go freelance. She asks you over lunch what you think of her decision. What do you tell her?
You are sitting at your desk on a Tuesday afternoon with two hours of routine work in front of you. Describe what goes through your mind as you work through it.
You wake up on a Monday with a full week ahead, nothing unusual scheduled, and no particular deadline. What is the first thing you feel, and what do you do?

A friend tells you he has been offered a lateral move at his company—different team, different work, same pay, same benefits, but no guarantee the new role will be better. He is not sure whether to take it or stay put where he knows the ropes. What do you say to him?
You are twelve years into a job and someone at a party asks you what you do. How do you answer, and what, if anything, do you leave out?
Your employer announces a new initiative that requires everyone to attend a two-day team-building retreat on a weekend in two months. How do you react, and what do you do about it?

You have the chance to take on a stretch assignment that would be visible and demanding but that falls entirely outside the work you find meaningful. Doing it well could accelerate your career; declining means staying in your current lane. What do you decide?
A younger family member is finishing university and asks you what factors you think matter most when choosing where to work. What do you say?

You get an email on a Friday afternoon letting you know that a project you lead has been pushed back by three weeks, meaning your workload this month is lighter than expected. How do you feel, and how do you spend the extra time?

You are passed over for a promotion that goes to someone with fewer years at the company. You have a performance review scheduled for next week. What do you plan to say, and what do you actually say when you get there?

A recruiter reaches out with a role that pays roughly the same as your current job but comes with no pension and would require you to give up five years of vested benefits. The work itself sounds more engaging. Do you respond, and if so what do you say?
Your closest friend at work resigns with no other job lined up, telling you she just could not face another year there. She asks if you ever think about doing the same. What do you tell her?
You have a week of annual leave approved. Monday arrives and you realize the office keeps messaging you with small requests. What do you do, and how does the week feel?
It is performance review season and your manager asks you to describe your five-year career goals. What do you say?

You are working on a long report that nobody senior will read closely. You are about halfway through and can see that the remaining sections will take another full day. What do you do with the second half?
Someone at a dinner party says that people who stay in jobs they dislike have only themselves to blame, since no one is forcing them to stay. What do you say in response?

Your company offers an early retirement package to anyone with more than ten years of service, but the payout is modest—enough to cover about eighteen months of expenses. You have fifteen years in. What do you do?

You are offered a secondment to another department for six months doing work that would be genuinely new to you, but it would interrupt your progress toward the next pension milestone. What do you decide?
A neighbour tells you she has just quit her stable corporate job to open a small shop, and she looks the happiest you have ever seen her. How does her news land with you, and what do you say?
It is a Wednesday afternoon and your calendar is clear for the next two hours. No meetings, no urgent deadlines. What do you do with the time, and what are you thinking?

Your mortgage comes up for renewal and you could either extend the term to reduce monthly payments or keep the current term and pay it off sooner. Which do you choose, and what is the reasoning behind it?
A younger colleague asks you privately whether you think the company is a good long-term place to build a career. What do you tell her?
Your department has started an optional Friday social event after work. Attendance is not required. What do you do, and how do you feel about going or not going?
You have been asked to mentor a new hire who is enthusiastic about the industry and full of questions about how to build a career here. What kind of advice do you give?
Your partner suggests the two of you take a significant pay cut and move somewhere cheaper, slower, and smaller, where you could both work less. What is your reaction, and what do you end up saying?

A close friend says he is miserable at work and is thinking about handing in his notice without another job lined up, convinced that the certainty of staying is worse than the uncertainty of leaving. What do you tell him?
You are in a meeting that has run long and is going nowhere. The room is waiting for a decision that could easily be postponed. What do you do?
You overhear two new hires talking excitedly about where they hope to be in the company in three years. What do you feel, and do you say anything to them?
Your employer announces a restructuring. Your role is not at risk, but the department around you will change significantly. How do you respond to the news, and what do you do in the following week?
You are filling in a form that asks you to list your occupation and a brief description of what you do. What do you write, and how long does it take you to decide?

A friend who left a secure job two years ago to start her own business tells you it has been harder than expected financially but that she does not regret it for a moment. She asks whether you have ever considered doing something similar. What do you say?
You have a rare free afternoon with nothing scheduled, no obligations, and no one expecting anything from you. What do you do with it, and what comes to mind?

You are offered a chance to transfer to a branch in a city you have always wanted to live in. The role is the same, the pay is the same, but the move would require selling the house and starting the mortgage process over. What do you do?
A colleague asks over coffee what you think the hardest part of your job actually is. What do you say?

You are in the middle of drafting a message to your manager asking about flexible working arrangements when you realize it might draw attention to the fact that you are disengaged. Do you send it, revise it, or drop it?
Someone you knew from university gets in touch and mentions he retrained completely at forty and now works in a field he loves for less money. He asks how things are going with you. What do you say?
You have just received your annual bonus. It is smaller than you hoped but still meaningful. What do you do with it, and what runs through your mind as you decide?

Your manager offers you the chance to lead a high-profile project that would require extra hours for the next four months but would significantly raise your profile in the company. What do you decide, and what goes into that decision?
